messages.author: 744ad518e240c51e
messages.subject: Not being positive definite
parts:
Dear lavaan users,

 

This is my first attempt of CFA, so any help is very much appreciated.


I have 9 observed variables; they can be grouped into three groups (3 in each) measuring 3 latent variables. I am trying to follow the logic of Miyake (2000) paper to show that there is commonality but also diversity of the three latent variables.  So the first step is to test following models: (1) three latent variables were orthogonal, fixed to 0 (diversity model); (2) three latent variable were perfectly correlated, fixed to 1 (unity model); (3) correlation between latent variables were free to estimate.

 

First, the model where latent covariance can be estimated freely converged without warnings.

modelC <-‘

updating =~ Task1 + Task4 + Task6

inhibition =~ Task3 + Task7 + Task9

shifting =~ Task2 + Task5 + Task8’

fit.modelC<- cfa(modelC, data = EF.data.M,)

 

However, when I tried to fit the model with orthogonal latent variables:

fit.modelC.orth<- cfa(modelC, data = EF.data.M, orthogonal = TRUE)

it generated warning messages “covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite” and “some estimated variances are negative”

 

I wonder what the problem is and how am I able to get around this? I have checked discussions about matrix not being positive definite. It has mentioned that this could be due to model misspecification or missing values which were not the case. Also it mentioned linear dependency could be a problem, this is neither the case, in addition, the fact that modelC without assuming orthogonality converged successfully means the covariance matrix is positive definite (am I correct with this?).

 

Many thanks in advance for any input/comment.

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: RE: Not being positive definite
parts:
First, if the freely estimated factor covariances were substantial, then the orthogonality model will be a very poor fit to the data, and very strange things can happen when the model is a very poor fit.  Second, with orthogonality constraints in place, statistical identification (the ability to obtain unique best estimates of parameters) in your model—with three indicators for each common factor—hinges on *every* factor loading being “large.”  If even one loading is not “large,” then identification fails, and you cannot trust output in any way.  There is no guarantee that you can obtain what you may call “good” estimates from the orthogonality model.

--Ed Rigdon

messages.author: 744ad518e240c51e
messages.subject: Re: Not being positive definite
parts:
Hi Ed,

thank you very much! This is very helpful for me to understand what is going on. 

It's true that according to literature the orthogonal model is not supposed to provide a good fit to the data. Regarding the second point, I am not experienced with SEM, what would be considered as 'large'? In the model where orthononality was not assumes, most indicators have a standard factor loading around .50 - .70, but 3 have a loading around .20 (I assumes this is not large). So I tried again with removing the 2 indicators with lowest loading, warning messages still come up. (Well, I guess there would be problem if each factor has only 2 indicators, I remembered reading that in the ideal world one would have at least 3 indicators for each factor). It appears both of the points that you brought up could have lead to this situation. 

A follow up question is then how can I report this? As I wished to compare model that assumes or does not assume orthogonality. With this outcome, is it still legal to do a model comparison, or shall I report that warning messages might be a sign of poor model fit and do not carry on with comparison.

Again many thanks in advance. This is very helpful!

Regards,
Beinan

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: Not being positive definite
parts:
Beinan--
     "Large" is something like "statistically significant," though significance is arbitrary, based on choice of alpha.  Basic identification rules are:

3 indicators per factor, or
2 indicators per factor, if each factor is correlated with something else (like another factor).

     My guess is that the weak Loadings mean that you cannot estimate the orthogonality model conventionally.  Given that, I do not have a way for you to achieve the kind of parallel that you want.
     As you guess, taking away an indicator with a weak loading does not help the problem.
     3 per factor is not "ideal" by any means.  It is just the minimum that achieves identification, without some other constraints being added.  More indicators is better for firmly establishing the factors.  (When you have time, search for the phrase, "factor indeterminacy.")
--Ed Rigdon

Sent from my iPad
